Featured Creatures

Clownfish

Clownfish live in sea anemones. They have a special slime on their skin that stops the anemone from stinging them!

Click to learn more

Angelfish

Angelfish are known for their bright colors and flat bodies, which help them slip through coral branches!

Click to learn more

Guppy

Guppies are famous for adapting to different environments rapidly and having highly colorful tails.

Click to learn more

Betta Fish

Betta fish can breathe air from the surface of the water using a special organ called a labyrinth.

Click to learn more

Catfish

Catfish get their name from the whisker-like barbels around their mouths, which they use to taste their surroundings.

Click to learn more

Salmon

Salmon can navigate back to the exact river where they were born using Earth's magnetic field.

Click to learn more

Trout

Trout are closely related to salmon and have beautiful spotted patterns along their sides.

Click to learn more

Bass

Bass are powerful swimmers that can quickly burst from hiding spots to catch their dinner.

Click to learn more

Perch

Perch have tough, rough scales and sharp fins that protect them from predators.

Click to learn more

Tilapia

Some species of tilapia protect their young by keeping them safe inside their mouths!

Click to learn more

Anchovy

Anchovies travel in enormous schools that sometimes contain millions of fish to stay safe.

Click to learn more

Pufferfish

Pufferfish can inflate into a ball shape to evade predators. They do this by quickly swallowing huge amounts of water!

Click to learn more

Lionfish

Lionfish are known for their beautiful, venomous spines. They are skilled hunters that corner their prey with their large fins.

Click to learn more

Swordfish

Swordfish use their long, flat bill to slash at schools of fish. They are one of the fastest swimmers in the ocean.

Click to learn more

Mackerel

Mackerel swim in large schools and migrate long distances. Their streamlined bodies make them excellent swimmers.

Click to learn more

Herring

Herring are a vital food source for many marine animals. They form massive schools that can contain billions of fish.

Click to learn more

Cod

Cod can live in very cold waters thanks to a special antifreeze protein in their blood. They are bottom-feeders.

Click to learn more

Flounder

Flounders are flatfish that lay on their sides on the ocean floor. Both of their eyes are on the same side of their head!

Click to learn more

Grouper

Groupers are heavy-bodied fish with large mouths. They swallow their prey whole instead of biting pieces off.

Click to learn more

Snapper

Snappers get their name from their large, sharp teeth. Many species are known for their bright red or pink colors.

Click to learn more

Barracuda

Barracudas are fierce predators known for their lightning-fast ambush attacks. They are attracted to shiny objects.

Click to learn more

Piranha

Piranhas have incredibly sharp teeth and powerful jaws. Despite their fierce reputation, many are actually vegetarians!

Click to learn more

Wrasse

Wrasses are very colorful and often act as "cleaner fish". They eat parasites off the bodies of larger fish.

Click to learn more

Parrotfish

Parrotfish use their beak-like teeth to scrape algae off coral. They actually poop fine white sand, which helps build beaches!

Click to learn more

Blenny

Blennies are small, bottom-dwelling fish with big eyes and a continuous dorsal fin. They often hide in empty shells or crevices.

Click to learn more

Goby

Gobies often form special friendships with pistol shrimps. The shrimp builds a burrow, and the goby acts as a lookout.

Click to learn more

Damselfish

Damselfish are known for fiercely defending their little patches of coral reef. Some species even "farm" their own algae!

Click to learn more

Filefish

Filefish have rough, sandpaper-like skin. They can change color rapidly to blend in with their surroundings.

Click to learn more

Triggerfish

Triggerfish can lock their dorsal fin spine in place to wedge themselves tightly into rock crevices, safe from predators.

Click to learn more

Pipefish

Pipefish are relatives of the seahorse. Like seahorses, it is the male pipefish that carries the eggs in a special pouch.

Click to learn more

Trumpetfish

Trumpetfish have long, tubular bodies and snout. They often swim vertically to disguise themselves among sea whips and coral.

Click to learn more

Needlefish

Needlefish swim right at the surface of the water. When frightened, they can leap out and skip along the surface at high speeds.

Click to learn more

Flying Fish

Flying fish have specially adapted, wing-like pectoral fins. They can launch out of the water and glide for hundreds of feet to escape predators.

Click to learn more

Moonfish

The moonfish, or opah, is the only known fully warm-blooded fish. This allows it to be a fast predator in cold, deep waters.

Click to learn more

Sunfish

The ocean sunfish (Mola mola) is the heaviest bony fish in the world. They love to lay flat on the surface to sunbathe!

Click to learn more

Sardine

Sardines travel in enormous, swirling schools. This "safety in numbers" tactic makes it hard for predators to target a single fish.

Click to learn more

Giant Pacific Octopus

This amazing creature has three hearts and blue blood! It can also change its color to hide from predators.

Click to learn more

Sea Pen

Sea pens look like old-fashioned quill pens sticking out of the sand. They are actually colonies of tiny animals called polyps.

Click to learn more

Sea Fan

Sea fans orient themselves to face the ocean currents. This helps their net-like structure catch as much drifting food as possible.

Click to learn more

Anemone

Sea anemones look like underwater flowers, but they are predatory animals. Their tentacles have tiny harpoons to catch passing fish.

Click to learn more

Sea Urchin

Sea urchins are covered in protective spines. Underneath, they have a complex jaw called "Aristotle’s lantern" to scrape algae.

Click to learn more

Sea Cucumber

Sea cucumbers act like the vacuum cleaners of the ocean floor. When threatened, some species can shoot sticky threads out of their bodies!

Click to learn more

Barnacle

Barnacles cement themselves to rocks, whales, and ships. They use feathery, leg-like appendages to sweep food into their mouths.

Click to learn more

Mussel

Mussels attach themselves to rocks using incredibly strong threads called "byssal threads," which are tougher than spider silk.

Click to learn more

Snail

Marine snails come in beautiful shells. Some predatory sea snails, like the cone snail, hunt fish using a venomous harpoon!

Click to learn more

Clam

Giant clams can live for over 100 years. They get much of their nutrition from algae that lives inside their colorful mantle tissue.

Click to learn more

Oyster

Oysters are incredible water filters. A single adult oyster can filter up to 50 gallons of water a day, keeping the ocean clean.

Click to learn more

Scallop

Unlike other bivalves, scallops can swim! They rapidly open and close their shells to jet-propel themselves away from starfish.

Click to learn more

Krill

These tiny, shrimp-like creatures are the main food source for the largest animals on Earth, including blue whales.

Click to learn more

Copepod

Copepods are tear-drop shaped zooplankton. They are often considered the most abundant multi-cellular animals on Earth!

Click to learn more

Amphipod

Amphipods are tiny crustaceans that lack a hard outer shell. Many are known as "scuds" or "sand hoppers" on beaches.

Click to learn more

Isopod

Deep-sea giant isopods are related to the roly-polys in your garden. The cold, deep water allows them to grow incredibly large.

Click to learn more

Horseshoe Crab

Horseshoe crabs are living fossils and are actually closer relatives to spiders and scorpions than they are to true crabs.

Click to learn more

Mantis Shrimp

Mantis shrimp have the most complex eyes in the animal kingdom. They can see colors that humans cannot even imagine.

Click to learn more

Hermit Crab

Hermit crabs must find larger shells as they grow. Sometimes they line up by size to swap shells in a chain reaction!

Click to learn more

Fiddler Crab

Male fiddler crabs have one oversized claw that they wave to attract mates. If they lose it, the smaller claw grows large to replace it!

Click to learn more

Spider Crab

The Japanese spider crab has the longest leg span of any arthropod. They are gentle giants that scavenge on the deep sea floor.

Click to learn more

Coconut Crab

Coconut crabs are massive land-dwelling hermit crabs. They use their incredibly powerful claws to crack open fallen coconuts.

Click to learn more

Sea Slug

Sea slugs lack a protective shell. Instead, many absorb toxins from their prey to make themselves poisonous to predators.

Click to learn more

Nudibranch

Nudibranchs are brightly colored sea slugs. Some can eat stinging anemones and store the stingers in their own bodies for defense!

Click to learn more

Sea Spider

Sea spiders are fascinating creatures that have no lungs or gills. Gases simply diffuse through their long, thin legs.

Click to learn more

Brittle Star

Brittle stars are related to starfish but have long, whip-like arms. They move surprisingly fast by wriggling their flexible arms.

Click to learn more

Bottlenose Dolphin

Dolphins are super smart and talk to each other using squeaks, whistles, and clicks. They even have names for each other!

Click to learn more

Porpoise

Porpoises are similar to dolphins but have shorter, rounder faces and smaller dorsal fins.

Click to learn more

Humpback Whale

Humpback whales are famous for their complex, beautiful songs, which can be heard for miles. They also love to leap out of the water in spectacular breaches.

Click to learn more

Blue Whale

The blue whale is the largest animal to have ever lived on Earth! Its tongue alone weighs as much as an elephant.

Click to learn more

Sperm Whale

Sperm whales have the largest brain of any animal. They dive incredibly deep to hunt for giant squid in the dark ocean depths.

Click to learn more

Beluga Whale

Beluga whales have extremely flexible necks, allowing them to turn their heads to look around. They are often called the "canaries of the sea" for their chirps.

Click to learn more

Narwhal

The narwhal is known as the "unicorn of the sea." Its famous tusk is actually a long, spiraled tooth packed with millions of nerve endings.

Click to learn more

Harbor Seal

Harbor seals often sleep in the water. They have a special reflex that slows their heart rate and lets them rest underwater for up to 30 minutes.

Click to learn more

Leopard Seal

Leopard seals are fierce predators of the Antarctic. They have powerful jaws and are the only seals known to regularly hunt penguins.

Click to learn more

Elephant Seal

Male elephant seals have a large, inflatable nose resembling an elephant's trunk. They use it to roar incredibly loud during mating season.

Click to learn more

Sea Lion

Unlike true seals, sea lions have visible ear flaps and can "walk" on land using their large front flippers.

Click to learn more

California Sea Lion

California sea lions are highly intelligent and playful. They are the acrobats of the sea and can often be seen surfing in waves.

Click to learn more

Steller Sea Lion

The Steller sea lion is the largest of all sea lions. A male can weigh as much as a small car and look like an underwater grizzly bear.

Click to learn more

Sea Otter

Sea otters have the thickest fur of any animal. They use rocks as tools to smash open hard-shelled prey like clams while floating on their backs.

Click to learn more

Manatee

Manatees are gentle herbivores, often called "sea cows." They spend up to 8 hours a day grazing on seagrass in shallow, warm waters.

Click to learn more

Dugong

Dugongs are cousins of manatees, but they have a fluked tail similar to a whale's. Legend says ancient sailors mistook them for mermaids.

Click to learn more

Walrus

Both male and female walruses have long ivory tusks. They use them to haul their massive bodies out of the water onto the ice.

Click to learn more

Great White Shark

Great whites are highly adapted predators that can sense a single drop of blood in 100 liters of water. They maintain a higher body temperature than the surrounding water.

Click to learn more

Tiger Shark

Tiger sharks have a reputation as the "garbage cans of the sea" because they will eat almost anything, including sea turtles, birds, and even old tires!

Click to learn more

Bull Shark

Unlike most sharks, bull sharks can survive in both saltwater and freshwater. They have been found swimming far up rivers like the Amazon and Mississippi.

Click to learn more

Nurse Shark

Nurse sharks are relatively slow-moving bottom dwellers. They use their strong jaws to suck conchs and crabs right out of their shells.

Click to learn more

Whale Shark

The whale shark is the largest fish in the sea, but it is a gentle filter feeder. It swims with its huge mouth open to catch tiny plankton.

Click to learn more

Hammerhead Shark

The unique shape of a hammerhead's head allows them to sweep the ocean floor like a metal detector to find hidden stingrays in the sand.

Click to learn more

Manta Ray

Manta rays are highly intelligent and have the largest brain-to-body ratio of any fish. They often visit "cleaning stations" where small fish remove their parasites.

Click to learn more

Stingray

Stingrays spend a lot of time buried in the sand to hide from predators. Their eyes are on top of their bodies, while their mouths are underneath!

Click to learn more

Eagle Ray

Eagle rays are spectacular swimmers that "fly" through the water with their large pectoral fins. They can even leap completely out of the ocean.

Click to learn more

Sawfish

Sawfish use their long, toothy snout to slash through schools of fish. They can also use it to pin prey against the ocean floor.

Click to learn more

Guitarfish

Guitarfish have a body that combines features of both a shark and a ray. They glide smoothly over the sand looking for crabs and worms.

Click to learn more

Skate

Skates look very much like stingrays, but they lack a stinging spine. They reproduce by laying leathery egg cases known as "mermaid's purses".

Click to learn more

Devil Ray

Devil rays get their name from the horn-like fins near their mouths. They form massive schools that travel together during migrations.

Click to learn more

Goblin Shark

The goblin shark has a prominent snout and can uniquely thrust its jaws outward to catch deep-sea prey in the blink of an eye.

Click to learn more

Frilled Shark

The frilled shark looks more like an eel or sea serpent than a shark. It has existed virtually unchanged for millions of years.

Click to learn more

Green Sea Turtle

Green sea turtles get their name not from their shells, but from their green fat, caused by a strict diet of seagrass and algae.

Click to learn more

Loggerhead Turtle

Loggerheads are named for their massive heads and strong jaws. They can easily crush the hard shells of conchs and crabs.

Click to learn more

Hawksbill Turtle

Hawksbills have a sharp, curving beak. They use it to carefully pick toxic sponges out of crevices in coral reefs.

Click to learn more

Leatherback Turtle

The leatherback is the largest sea turtle and lacks a hard bony shell. They can dive deeper than most whales in search of jellyfish.

Click to learn more

Sea Snake

Sea snakes are highly venomous but generally very docile. They have special valves that seal their nostrils when diving underwater.

Click to learn more

Nautilus

The nautilus is an ancient cephalopod with a chambered shell. It pumps gas into these chambers to float, acting like a natural submarine.

Click to learn more

Sea Dragon

Sea dragons are closely related to seahorses but cannot curl their tails. They drift lazily in the currents, looking exactly like seaweed.

Click to learn more

Leafy Sea Dragon

Covered in elaborate leaf-like attachments over their whole body, they are virtually invisible among kelp.

Click to learn more

Seahorse

Seahorses are the only animal where the male becomes pregnant. The father carries the eggs in a special brood pouch until they hatch.

Click to learn more

Anglerfish

Deep-sea anglerfish have a glowing lure on their head created by bioluminescent bacteria. They use it like a fishing rod to attract prey.

Click to learn more

Lanternfish

Lanternfish have rows of glowing organs along their bellies. They migrate to the surface at night to feed and return to the depths by day.

Click to learn more

Viperfish

Viperfish have fangs so long they cannot fit inside their mouths. Their transparent bodies make them almost invisible in the deep sea.

Click to learn more

Gulper Eel

The gulper eel has massive, loosely hinged jaws that allow it to swallow prey much larger than itself in the scarce deep sea environment.

Click to learn more

Dumbo Octopus

The dumbo octopus lives deeper than any other octopus species. It uses its ear-like fins to "fly" gracefully through the dark water.

Click to learn more

Vampire Squid

Despite its name, the vampire squid doesn't drink blood. Instead of shooting ink, it confuses predators by releasing a cloud of glowing mucus!

Click to learn more

Barreleye Fish

The barreleye fish has a completely transparent head! Its glowing green eyes look upward through its head to spot shadows of prey above.

Click to learn more

Fangtooth Fish

The fangtooth has the largest teeth of any fish in the ocean relative to body size. Its teeth are so big it has special pockets in its mouth to sheath them.

Click to learn more

Oarfish

The giant oarfish is the longest bony fish in the world and is thought to be the origin of many "sea serpent" legends.

Click to learn more

Blobfish

The blobfish has no muscles and relies on its gelatinous body to float just above the sea floor. In its deep habitat, the pressure keeps it looking like a normal fish!

Click to learn more

Brain Coral

Brain coral forms enormous, dome-shaped colonies. The intricate grooves make it look exactly like a human brain.

Click to learn more

Staghorn Coral

Staghorn coral is one of the most important reef-building corals in the Caribbean. Its branching arms provide shelter for hundreds of fish species.

Click to learn more

Fan Coral

Sea fans are flexible corals that bend with the ocean currents rather than breaking. They catch tiny floating food in their net-like branches.

Click to learn more

Soft Coral

Unlike hard corals, soft corals do not build rocky skeletons. They sway gracefully in the ocean waves and resemble underwater trees.

Click to learn more

Elkhorn Coral

Elkhorn coral branches look like giant moose antlers. It grows very fast and is critical for protecting coastlines from storm waves.

Click to learn more

Table Coral

Table coral grows in large, flat plates that look like underwater tables. This broad shape helps it capture as much sunlight as possible.

Click to learn more

Branching Coral

Branching corals have fragile tips that can easily snap off. The broken pieces often settle on the bottom and grow into entirely new coral colonies!

Click to learn more

Bubble Coral

During the day, bubble coral inflates grape-like vesicles filled with water to absorb sunlight. At night, it shrinks the bubbles and extends tentacles to feed.

Click to learn more

Mushroom Coral

Mushroom corals are unusual because they are a single, giant polyp rather than a colony. They are also free-living and not attached to the sea floor.

Click to learn more

Plate Coral

Plate corals overlap like shingles on a roof. This layered growth ensures that every level receives enough sunlight for photosynthesis.

Click to learn more

Kelp

Kelp isn't actually a plant—it's a type of large brown algae! It uses root-like structures called holdfasts to grip rocks securely.

Click to learn more

Giant Kelp

Giant kelp is one of the fastest-growing organisms on Earth. In ideal conditions, it can grow up to 2 feet in a single day!

Click to learn more

Sea Grass

Sea grasses are the only true plants that live entirely underwater. They produce flowers and even have tiny underwater seeds.

Click to learn more

Seaweed

Many types of seaweed contain special gels that are extracted and used in everyday human products like toothpaste and ice cream.

Click to learn more

Sea Lettuce

Sea lettuce is a bright green algae that thrives in shallow pools. It is fully edible and rich in nutrients.

Click to learn more

Dulse

Dulse is a reddish-purple seaweed that grows rapidly in cold waters. When pan-fried, many people say it smells and tastes like bacon.

Click to learn more

Nori

Nori is famously used around the world to wrap sushi. It is actually a type of red algae that turns dark green when dried.

Click to learn more

Sea Moss

Sea moss is a spiny red algae that is packed with vitamins. It acts as a natural thickening agent in many foods.

Click to learn more

Eelgrass

Eelgrass beds are essential nurseries for baby fish and crabs. The grass also helps trap sediment, keeping the ocean water clear.

Click to learn more

Turtle Grass

As the name suggests, turtle grass is the favorite meal of the green sea turtle. Its deep roots help anchor the sea floor during heavy storms.

Click to learn more

Mangrove

Mangroves are incredible trees that can survive in salty ocean water. Their tangled root systems provide safe hiding spots for thousands of young sea animals.

Click to learn more

Sea Blades

Sea blades refer to various broad-leaf algae. They are incredibly tough and rubbery to withstand the crashing power of ocean waves.

Click to learn more

Coralline Algae

Coralline algae is unique because it deposits calcium carbonate in its cell walls. This gives it a hard, rock-like texture that helps glue coral reefs together.

Click to learn more

Red Algae

Red algae can live deeper in the ocean than any other type of algae. Their red pigment allows them to absorb the faint blue light that penetrates deep water.

Click to learn more

Green Algae

Green algae are the ancestors of all modern land plants! They thrive in shallow water where they can soak up the maximum amount of sunlight.

Click to learn more

Ocean Explorer for Kids — Dive Into the Deep Sea & Discover Marine Life

Welcome to Ocean Explorer, the ultimate interactive learning experience for kids! Dive deep into the ocean and discover fascinating marine life, from colorful coral reefs to the mysterious deep sea.

What You'll Discover in Ocean Explorer

  • Interactive profiles of your favorite sea creatures.
  • Beautiful illustrations of marine life in their natural habitats.

Amazing Ocean Facts for Kids

  • The ocean covers more than 70% of the Earth's surface.
  • There are thousands of marine species yet to be discovered.
  • Coral reefs are home to 25% of all marine life.
  • The blue whale is the largest animal ever known to have lived on Earth.
